ogTitle: 10 Popular Restaurants in Sisaket 2026 — Eat Like a Local
ogDesc: Old-town Vietnamese kuay jab, Mae Sri roundabout breakfasts, fiery Isan food, seafood, and a paddy field café — 10 standout spots in Sisaket worth trying
intro: Sisaket is a city where great food runs from dawn to late night. It shines for its Vietnamese kuay jab, Mae Sri roundabout breakfasts, and punchy Isan flavours. We've gathered 10 restaurants that locals actually visit and travellers keep coming back to — legendary old-timers and newer spots with great atmosphere alike. Read through and you'll know exactly where to start.

blocks.html:
Any food story about Sisaket starts around the old-town district near Mae Sri Roundabout and the City Pillar Shrine — this is the heart of the city. Walk out first thing in the morning and rows of breakfast shops greet you within a few steps, the air thick with the scent of old-style coffee, sizzling pan eggs, and Vietnamese kuay jab. That Vietnamese-style kuay jab is Sisaket's signature dish: chewy, tender noodles in a clear, fragrant broth with a dab of roasted chilli paste — a flavour you won't easily find elsewhere. By mid-morning the action shifts toward the Big C area and the ring road, where you'll find fiery Isan eateries, grilled pork neck joints, Southern-style rice-and-curry shops, seafood, and paddy field cafés — a full day of eating without a dull moment.

This list includes legendary institutions that have anchored the city for decades: Jiao Ki, the 80-year-old breakfast house right at Mae Sri Roundabout, famous for Vietnamese kuay jab and pan-egg sets; and Pherm Phol (2506), the noodle shop that hand-rolls its own egg noodles daily over a duck palo broth — a recipe so beloved it's appeared on multiple national TV food programmes. For heat seekers, Tam Krathoey inside Big C draws a crowd for its seafood salads and fried chicken, while the evening stretches to Crossbow Grilled Pork Neck, Pu Pen seafood, P. Pak Tai Southern-style curries, Kuay Jab Khon Hen, and finally PoonNa Café for a paddy view wind-down. Pick up some Moo Yor Dao Phet sausage before you leave. Scroll down to explore each spot — Sisaket eats better than you think.

blocks.name: Jiao Ki Breakfast
blocks.signature: Vietnamese kuay jab, pan-egg set, old-style coffee, pa thong ko
blocks.descHtml:
When Sisaket locals think of breakfast in the city centre, "Jiao Ki" comes to mind first — an 80-year-old shophouse canteen right at Mae Sri Roundabout on the main road, just behind the train station. Generations of Sisaket families have brought guests here for the first meal of the day. Step off the morning train and you're there in a few steps. The setting keeps its old-era charm and the prices won't strain your wallet.

The most-ordered item is the pan-egg set: a hot skillet loaded with moo yor pork sausage, Chinese sausage, and cracked pepper, served with crispy toast for dipping. Many guests also love the Vietnamese kuay jab — reviewers consistently describe it as "fragrant, well-rounded broth, chewy noodles, generous toppings for the price." Sweet-tooth diners can add hot rice porridge and pa thong ko, and the must-not-miss old-style coffee and iced tea are praised as being perfectly brewed in the traditional shophouse way. Beyond these classics, the menu also covers blood soup, rice porridge, American-style fried rice, and single-dish mains.

Prices are very reasonable — averaging under 100 THB per head, with pan eggs around 61 THB and American fried rice around 91 THB. Free water and tea are included. The space is large, airy, and cleaner than some might expect, decorated in classic shophouse style. Long-time regulars who return after years away still find the quality holding steady.

One thing to know: the shop opens very early, around 05:30–06:00, and closes mid-afternoon around 13:30. Come during the morning-to-late-morning window, as some dishes sell out fast. Parking around the roundabout is limited — if you're driving, budget a few extra minutes to find a spot.
blocks.bestFor: First breakfast in Sisaket — great straight off the train

blocks.name: Pherm Phol (2506) Homemade Egg Noodles
blocks.area: Mueang Nuea Sub-district, Mueang Sisaket District, Sisaket
blocks.signature: Homemade egg noodles in duck palo broth, red-roast pork and crispy pork on rice, hoi jo
blocks.descHtml:
If you're in Sisaket and want the noodle place locals call a true institution, Pherm Phol (2506) Homemade Egg Noodles is the name that comes up first. Open since 1963 and now in its third generation, the shop's calling card is egg noodles kneaded and rolled in-house every day — no colouring, no preservatives — giving them a springy, chewy texture that's hard to find at ordinary noodle shops. It sits near the City Pillar Shrine, making it an ideal stop for a warm late-morning or lunchtime bowl on the way around the old town.

The most popular order is duck noodles topped with a deep, aromatic palo sauce brewed to an old recipe; reviewers say the broth "needs almost no seasoning." You get tender duck meat, holy basil, Chinese celery, and crispy pork crumble. Those who prefer straight noodles can order wonton bah mee or mixed bah mee for around 50 THB. Rice-eaters can choose red-roast pork, crispy pork, or duck-on-rice. The not-to-miss nibble is old-recipe hoi jo — crispy fried and firm moo yor.

The atmosphere is a relaxed old shophouse with plenty of tables. Fresh coffee is available to pair with your morning bowl. Average spend is under 100 THB — good value for everything made in-house. The shop is on Theppha Road, a short walk from the City Pillar Shrine, with street parking nearby. Open daily from 08:30 to 15:30.

What keeps Pherm Phol in Sisaket hearts after all these decades is the unwavering consistency of flavour and the daily hand-rolled noodles. The shop has won provincial "local speciality" awards and appeared on several national food TV programmes. Worth knowing: the shop closes in the afternoon and focuses on dine-in. Come before noon to get the freshest noodles and the full menu experience.
mustOrder: Red-roast pork and crispy pork on rice
blocks.bestFor: Morning-to-lunch bowl of homemade noodles in the old town

blocks.name: Tam Krathoey Sisaket
blocks.area: Inside Big C, Mueang Sisaket District
blocks.signature: Seafood salad / blue crab salad, Krathoey fried chicken, forest-style som tam, fried pork ribs, fresh prawn pad thai
blocks.descHtml:
If you want fiery Isan som tam without hunting around, Tam Krathoey inside Sisaket Big C is where locals head. It belongs to the Tam Krathoey Sakaet brand — an Isan folk-food chain that grew from Roi Et and now has branches across the region — so the flavour is consistent, while each bowl of som tam is still freshly pounded to order. Good for families and groups: spacious, easy Big C parking, no headache finding a spot.

Popular orders include the seafood salad and blue crab salad — fresh seafood tossed in a punchy, sour-spicy dressing. For fried items, try the Krathoey fried chicken (crispy skin, tender meat) and pork ribs, both great with the jaew dipping sauce. Forest-style som tam comes loaded with vegetables and fermented fish aroma. Fresh prawn pad thai offers a flavour break from the richness. Other highlights: the tamuang-phlua salad and young bamboo soup with red ant eggs in true Isan style.

Most reviews agree: the ingredients are genuinely fresh, the flavour is authentically Isan — not watered down — the staff are warm, and the décor has a folk-Isan feel. Price runs 101–250 THB per head; single-portion som tam is cheap, while seafood dishes like crab salad go higher depending on market price.

The shop is inside Big C, open daily around 10:30–20:30. Works for both lunch and dinner. It gets busy in the evenings and on weekends when shoppers stop in. Tell the staff if you want the chilli turned down, and for seafood dishes come early in the day for the fullest selection.
blocks.bestFor: A spicy group meal with family or friends while doing a Big C run
blocks.libCredit: Illustrative photo: som tam · Vyacheslav Argenberg / Wikimedia (CC BY 4.0)

blocks.name: Jaruad Breakfast
blocks.signature: Pork rice porridge, fish rice porridge, kuay jab, pan-egg set, American fried rice
blocks.descHtml:
If you wake up in Sisaket unsure where to start the day, Jaruad Breakfast is the place locals point you to almost automatically. It sits right at Mae Sri Roundabout, next to the entrance of Wat Phra To, smack in the middle of town — easy to find. Open for years, it counts as one of the province's classic morning haunts, with a menu spanning everything from light bites to full à la carte mains. Perfect for groups with different tastes, or anyone wanting a hearty warm-up before heading out.

Popular orders include pork rice porridge with egg, fish congee, Vietnamese kuay jab, pan-egg set, and American fried rice. Reviews praise the fish congee for its clear, rounded broth; the kuay jab gets full marks for generous noodles. For something more substantial, stir-fried sea bass with Chinese celery and blood soup with clean offal are singled out as better than expected. Hot Chinese tea arrives free while you wait.

Prices are very accessible — single dishes from around 30–95 THB, a loaded pan-egg set around 140 THB, average spend well under the low hundreds. The room is open-plan, breezy along the street, with photogenic corners to snap a shot. Opens very early around 5:30 and runs into early afternoon — good for early risers and late-morning sleepers alike.

Worth knowing: the shop is right at a busy roundabout, so mornings are traffic-heavy and parking is tight. Some reviews note the American fried rice is on the plain side and the tomato sauce a touch too tart — but with such a broad menu, wallet-friendly prices, and its status as a Sisaket morning institution, it remains a worthy first stop.
blocks.bestFor: First meal in town before heading out
blocks.libCredit: Illustrative photo: rice porridge · Alpha from Melbourne, Australia / Wikimedia (CC BY-SA 2.0)

blocks.name: Pu Pen Sisaket
blocks.area: Town centre, Mueang Sisaket District (near Somdet Park)
blocks.signature: Fresh live crab, oysters, prawn cakes, sour curry with riwkiu fish roe, marinated crab / steamed crab
blocks.descHtml:
Pu Pen Sisaket brings the freshness of the sea to a landlocked Isan province. Crab, prawns, squid, and oysters are sourced from the Surat Thani area, delivering a level of freshness that's rare this far inland. Ideal for families wanting a full seafood feast, groups who want to gather around a pot of hot steamed crab, or anyone craving the ocean without the long drive.

Nearly every table orders the fresh live crab — both steamed and marinated — the sweet, plump meat is the highlight. That's followed by large oysters, springy prawn cakes, and a sour curry with riwkiu fish roe that leads with a clean tartness. For those who like heat, prawn-and-roe yam and crab salad are worth a try. Reviews consistently call the seafood "fresh as claimed" — no fishy smell, punchy dipping sauce, big plump prawns, sweet oysters. Many say it genuinely tastes like the sea: fresh, clean, and worth the price.

The atmosphere is relaxed, family-style — comfortable seating, smiley staff who check in at your table throughout the meal, with several reviewers praising the cook's warm personality. Prices are fair for fresh seafood, averaging 250–500 THB per head; a crab fried rice starts in the low hundreds, while whole crabs and prawns are priced by weight.

Location is in the old town, Mueang Nuea sub-district, on Khukhon Road near Wat Phra To (Wat Maha Phuttharam) and close to Somdet Park — easy to get to with convenient parking. Open daily approximately 10:30–19:30. Because it's one of the few places in town with genuinely fresh seafood every day, evenings and weekends see early sellouts of the best crabs and prawns. Come mid-morning to early afternoon, or call ahead to reserve.
mustOrder: Sour curry with riwkiu fish roe
blocks.zone: Old town (near Wat Phra To / Somdet Park)

blocks.name: P. Pak Tai Branch 3 Sisaket
blocks.signature: Southern-style rice and curry, kaeng tai pla / kaeng som, khua kling, stir-fried sataw beans
blocks.descHtml:
For a full, honest plate of Southern curry at a price you don't need to think twice about, P. Pak Tai Branch 3 is the name Sisaket locals pass around. The shop sits on the Sisaket–Uthumphon Phisai road in Tambon Ya Plong, about 200 metres from Big C in the same stretch as Prince Sisaket Hospital — a landmark easy to spot. A mother-and-daughter team has run this Southern curry shop for nearly 20 years, making it one of the city's largest curry shops with the most choice. Perfect for a quick, satisfying lunch or a group that wants something to share — with over 50 dishes on the counter to choose from.

The star is the Southern cooking using curry paste ordered direct from the South blended with the house recipe. Must-orders: kaeng tai pla (turmeric-fish curry) with its bold, fiery depth, khua kling with its fragrant curry-paste perfume, and stir-fried sataw beans, loved by regulars. Those who prefer mild can find sweet pork, egg in palo sauce, coconut chicken soup, thepho curry, pineapple curry, catfish red curry, and much more. Reviews regularly praise the depth and generosity of flavour — and they scoop rice high.

Pricing is extremely friendly: one curry over rice 40 THB, two dishes 50 THB, with rice and an extra side 60 THB, a cup of curry around 50 THB, dessert around 25 THB. The setting is a casual, open canteen — not fancy, but clean and fast. The shop is also known in the community as a halal option.

Open every day with no days off, roughly 08:00–16:00, with lunch as the main focus. Be aware that popular dishes like kaeng tai pla and khua kling tend to run out around noon. Come before the lunch rush if you want everything, and expect it to be busy during peak hours. Street parking is available outside.
blocks.libCredit: Illustrative photo: curry · Takeaway / Wikimedia (CC BY-SA 3.0)

blocks.name: Crossbow Grilled Pork Neck Sisaket
blocks.signature: Grilled pork neck, nam tok grilled pork neck, crispy pork, three-layer deep-fried pork with fish sauce, spicy leng soup
blocks.descHtml:
For grilled pork neck in Sisaket, Crossbow Grilled Pork Neck is the name serious fans look for. A small, casual spot with a raw-charming wood-and-corrugated-iron interior, tucked in Soi Khukhon 1 in the southern town area — easy to find near the centre. Works equally well solo, with friends, or as a family evening chill.

The star is the freshly grilled pork neck — cut from low-fat collar, marinated with galangal, lemongrass, and kaffir lime leaves, then charcoal-grilled until the surface is hazy and aromatic while the meat stays tender. Reviews are unanimous that it pairs beautifully with the kaffir lime leaf jaew dipping sauce. Other regulars: nam tok pork neck salad (spicy and savoury), crispy three-layer pork with fish sauce, and a big pot of spicy leng soup that delivers both heat and satisfaction. Those after something different can try the southern-style braised pork belly.

Pricing is very generous — grilled pork neck starts in the low hundreds; fried and stewed dishes under a hundred to low hundreds. Two or three items between a table and you're full without straining the wallet. A fun detail: check in at the shop and you often get a complimentary palm sugar coconut sticky rice dessert to finish.

The shop runs from late morning to midnight daily — works for lunch, dinner, and late-night cravings alike. Seating both inside and outside. Busy evenings on weekends, so call ahead or arrive before peak if you don't want to wait. The freshly grilled pork neck takes a few minutes on the grill but it's absolutely worth the heat and aroma.
mustOrder: Three-layer pork fried with fish sauce
blocks.bestFor: Evening or late-night spicy meal on a budget

blocks.name: Kuay Jab Khon Hen
blocks.signature: Vietnamese kuay jab with roasted chilli paste, jumbo braised chicken feet
blocks.descHtml:
If you're in Sisaket and want a kuay jab experience unlike the usual, Kuay Jab Khon Hen is the first name locals tend to bring up. This is Vietnamese-style kuay jab made with flat rice noodles — soft and slightly chewy — not the clear-broth version many are used to. The draw is a slightly thick, concentrated broth with hints of mild palo from slow-braised chicken feet, giving every bowl both fragrance and depth in one go. Right for people who love bold flavour, generous toppings, and a local dish hard to find elsewhere.

The must-order is the Vietnamese kuay jab with roasted chilli paste — the shop's signature. Their roasted chilli paste has a distinctive kaffir lime fragrance; stir it in and the broth jumps up a notch. The bowl comes with ground pork, sliced moo yor, egg, and the star: tender braised chicken feet. Hungry? Go for the jumbo bowl — the toppings fill it completely. Many reviews say the broth is so full-flavoured it barely needs seasoning.

Pricing is very wallet-friendly: a regular bowl around 45 THB, special 50 THB, jumbo 60 THB — a satisfying meal for well under a hundred baht. The shop is on Theppha Road in Mueang Nuea sub-district, across from the City Pillar Shrine, diagonally from the 7-Eleven at the City Pillar — easy to find, easy to park. The evening branch opens around 17:00 until 22:30, Monday to Friday. A separate lunchtime branch also operates for midday visits.

The shop's reputation comes from its distinct style of kuay jab that's hard to find anywhere else, plus consistently priced-right portions. Worth knowing: the evening branch is closed on weekends. If you're making a trip specifically for this, confirm the day beforehand — and at peak times expect a short queue.
mustOrder: Vietnamese kuay jab with roasted chilli paste
Jumbo bowl with braised chicken feet
blocks.bestFor: Evening bowl of bold local kuay jab on a budget

blocks.name: Moo Yor Dao Phet
blocks.signature: Moo yor, Chinese sausage, Isan sausage, cartilage naem, moo sawan, sour fish
blocks.descHtml:
Ask any Sisaket local where to buy souvenirs and Moo Yor Dao Phet comes up near the top. This shop has been making and selling moo yor since 1973 — over fifty years now — the first of its kind in the province, and it has held its place in the hearts of every generation of Sisaket residents. The perfect stop for anyone wanting to bring something genuinely local home, or travellers who want to taste the real original — not market imitations.

The star product is the skin-on moo yor: firm, springy, with just the right amount of skin — chewy and satisfying. Anyone who likes traditional-style must try it. Beyond moo yor, there's sweetly fragrant Chinese sausage, tangy Isan sausage, cartilage naem with its sour-crunchy bite, sweet-salty moo sawan, and punchy traditional-style sour fish. Multiple customers say everything they pick up is delicious, the flavour is honest, and products are made fresh daily since everything is made and sold in-house.

The shop is a shophouse on Theppha Road, across from the Mueang Nuea Post Office — street parking available. The setting is a simple souvenir shop, not fancy, but the display cases are full and browsing is easy. Prices are friendly: small pieces start in the dozens of baht, bundles still won't break the bank. Open from early morning (six o'clock) until evening: Mon–Sat closes at 18:00, Sunday closes earlier at 17:00.

This shop has kept its loyal following for decades because of consistency — the flavour never wavers, everything is made fresh and sold fresh, and it's a name Sisaket locals are proud to bring to people in other provinces. Worth knowing: during festivals and long weekends the shop is busy and products sell out fast. If you plan to buy in bulk, call ahead to reserve or come early in the morning to get everything without the anxiety.
blocks.bestFor: Picking up souvenirs to take home
blocks.spice: Both mild and bold options available (sour fish / naem)

blocks.name: PoonNa Cafe and Eatery KM.8
blocks.area: Khayung Sub-district, Uthumphon Phisai District, Sisaket
blocks.signature: Coffee drinks, bakery, light meals, with paddy field views
blocks.descHtml:
PoonNa Cafe and Eatery KM.8 is a café set in the middle of rice fields, just about 8 kilometres from Sisaket town toward Uthumphon Phisai, on Nong Yang Village Road in Khayung sub-district. For anyone wanting to escape the noise and sit with a coffee overlooking endless green, this is the answer. The café is divided into several seating zones: an air-conditioned indoor area and an outdoor zone along the paddies where a breeze blows all day. Works for solo chilling, couples, or groups of friends and family settling in for a long stretch.

Popular orders lean toward the iced coffee and blended drinks — caramel macchiato blended and iced cappuccino, both around fifty-something baht a glass. Bakery fans can pick at chocolate cake and toasted bread for a relaxed snack. Those wanting something more substantial can order single-dish mains: pork rad na, prawn fried rice, and a punchy Isan-style som tam. Most menu items stay under 100 THB — coffee, snacks, and a full meal all in one spot, easy on the wallet.

Customer reviews all point to atmosphere as the selling point: "amazing view, tons of photo spots" and "there's always a breeze." Sitting and eating surrounded by green paddy fields delivers a sense of calm you can't find in the city. Multiple photo-friendly spots set up around the property; wide parking lot and free Wi-Fi; easy to reach.

The café is open daily 09:00–18:00. In the midday heat the outdoor zone can get warm; early morning or late afternoon gives the best atmosphere and light. For the deepest green paddy colour, visit during the rainy season to early cool season — the fields are lush and full, which is exactly what turns this small roadside café into the favourite roadside stop on the Sisaket–Uthumphon Phisai stretch.
blocks.bestFor: Café lovers who want paddy field views and a chill photo session

blocks.title: Good to know before eating in Sisaket

items.title: Getting around town
items.text: Grab is scarce in Sisaket city and wait times are long. Renting a car or motorbike is the most flexible option. The morning breakfast spots around Mae Sri Roundabout and the City Pillar Shrine are walkable from each other, but out-of-town spots like PoonNa Café require your own wheels.

items.title: Bring cash
items.text: Most street food and breakfast shops accept cash or PromptPay only — no card. Keep small bills on hand. Larger mall-based spots like Tam Krathoey and some cafés offer scan-to-pay.

items.title: Go early or avoid the rush
items.text: Legendary breakfast spots like Jiao Ki sell out fast and close in the afternoon — aim to arrive before 9am. Evening spots fill up on holiday weekends; arrive before 6pm for an easier table.

items.title: Menus are mostly Thai
items.text: Most local spots have Thai-only menus and minimal English. A translation app or pointing at food photos goes a long way. The words kuay jab yuan (Vietnamese kuay jab) and khai kratha (pan-egg set) will get you the signature dishes.

items.title: State your spice level upfront
items.text: Isan food and som tam here are genuinely spicy. If you can't handle heat, say "phet noi" (a little spicy) or "mai phet" (not spicy) when you order. Tam Krathoey and other som tam shops can adjust — you'll enjoy the meal far more without the suffering.

items.title: Tipping
items.text: Street food and breakfast shops have no tipping custom — pay the posted price. At table-service restaurants, a small tip or rounding up is a kind gesture that staff appreciate, but it's entirely optional.

blocks.title: How to plan a full day of eating in Sisaket
blocks.html:
Start early in the Mae Sri Roundabout area — Jiao Ki opens at 5:30am and sells out fast. Order the Vietnamese kuay jab and pan-egg set with old-style coffee. If you want to try the homemade noodles too, swing by Pherm Phol (2506) near the City Pillar Shrine around mid-morning, since that shop only runs until afternoon.

For lunch into early evening, head toward the Big C zone and ring road. Tam Krathoey is best shared in a group — order the seafood salad and fried chicken. P. Pak Tai is a cheap, easy Southern curry drop-in. Later in the evening, settle in at Crossbow Grilled Pork Neck or Pu Pen seafood for a long sit-down. Before leaving, stop at Moo Yor Dao Phet for moo yor and Isan sausage to take home. If you have time to spare, drive out toward Uthumphon Phisai and end the day with a coffee overlooking the paddy fields at PoonNa Café.

blocks.text: If you're visiting Sisaket and want to stroll out for morning Vietnamese kuay jab without the rush, staying in the town centre near Mae Sri Roundabout and Somdet Park is the most convenient choice — breakfast shops and the market are all within walking distance. Book ahead during the volcanic durian season for better rates.

faq.q: Which restaurant is the most famous in Sisaket?
faq.a: Jiao Ki is the legendary spot people mention most — an 80-year-old breakfast house right at Mae Sri Roundabout, known for Vietnamese kuay jab, pan-egg sets, and old-style coffee. Pherm Phol (2506) is just as celebrated for its homemade noodles and has appeared on multiple national TV food programmes.

The city's signature dish is Vietnamese kuay jab: chewy flat noodles in a clear, fragrant broth — find it at Jiao Ki and Kuay Jab Khon Hen. Other staples include the Mae Sri Roundabout breakfast scene (pan eggs, rice porridge, congee) and fiery Isan food like som tam and grilled pork neck.

faq.q: How much does eating in Sisaket cost?
faq.a: Breakfast and noodle dishes run about 30–140 THB per plate. Southern curry at P. Pak Tai starts as low as 40–60 THB. Group meals at Tam Krathoey are around 101–250 THB per head, and seafood at Pu Pen runs 250–500 THB per person depending on what you order.

faq.q: Do Sisaket restaurants require advance reservations?
faq.a: Most breakfast and noodle spots are walk-in — just sit down. But for large groups visiting Tam Krathoey or Pu Pen seafood in the evening on a weekend, calling ahead to book a table is a good idea since both get busy.

faq.q: Which spots are open in the evening or late at night?
faq.a: Crossbow Grilled Pork Neck and Pu Pen seafood are both solid evening choices. Tam Krathoey inside Big C stays open until late evening. Meanwhile, breakfast spots like Jiao Ki and Pherm Phol close in the afternoon — if you want those, go in the morning.
